thread.title: Head offshore with confidence - NewsBreak

author: Staff Writer
title: Head offshore with confidence - NewsBreak
text: It’s that time of year to head offshore for big fish, particularly if you like to cook and eat what you catch. If you have not ventured far offshore before, there are some things you can do and some electronics you can buy to give yourself more confidence. Yes, mechanical problems can possibly arise. Ideally, an offshore boat will have more than one outboard. However, most people with “do-everything” boats only have a single outboard, for the simple reason that having more than one usually means your boat would be bigger and heavier making fishing inshore in shallow water difficult. Having only a single outboard means you must make sure your engine is in excellent condition and up to date on routine maintenance, and that you are alert to potential issues before they develop into actual problems. I don’t profess to be an expert on boats, but I pamper my single outboard and there are some things that I have done to give me more confidence for 40- or 50-mile runs. I periodically add a gas stabilizer when filling the tank to help prevent moisture and water from accumulating in the tank. Like most, I have two starting batteries acquired at the same time. When one goes bad, I replace them both with the theory that the second one will probably fail sooner than later. I watch all my gauges for any indication of a potential problem. For example, although my Yamaha battery gauge did not indicate any battery problem, I noticed on my MFD that the battery voltage output while cruising was lower than its usual 13.8 to 14.3 volts. I brought it in for service and the tech confirmed the batteries were not charging properly, and I needed a new rectifier and regulator assembly on the outboard. Recently, I had my 2018 boat in for its usual 100-hour maintenance and the mechanic found that the seals in the lower unit were worn and water had entered. I was going to only have the seals replaced, but upon closer inspection the mechanic showed me some pitting on the main shaft. It might be fine for many more hours, but I wouldn’t feel comfortable making a long run with a main shaft that had a chance breaking — so I bit the bullet and had the entire lower unit replaced. Hey, it’s only money, right? If you want a cheap hobby, take up poetry. I carry a good assortment of safety gear on board: Life jackets, hand flares, a flare gun, a VHF radio, a backup handheld VHF, lights that can emit a strong SOS at night, and a daytime distress flag. I even have a portable jump-starting battery. If you get one of these, just make sure you know which is battery is which, so you put the cables on the right terminals before jumping the outboard. I didn’t want to try to figure this out during an emergency, so I had the service center label my batteries to be sure. Once I had confidence in the mechanics of my boat and safety gear, I ventured offshore gradually. At first I went only as far as Tremblay Reef, which seemed way offshore at the time but is only 6 miles from the beach. Then I ventured out to Power Pole Reef, Charlotte’s Reef and the Palm Island Ferry, which is about 13 miles out. All of these spots are routine now. However, to venture out further, I would have to cut the cord and go outside the range of my cell phone. To do this, I acquired additional safety gear. These devices are what gave me more confidence to do long offshore runs and are the subject of my next column.
